items.title: Lab 01 — Serve a model inside your boundary
items.audience: Platform and infrastructure engineers; anyone who has to answer "where does our data go when someone prompts the model?"
items.prerequisites: LAB_MODE=simulate: nothing. LAB_MODE=live: a RHEL host with a supported accelerator and CDI devices generated (nvidia-ctk cdi generate), podman, huggingface-cli, curl and jq on the path, registry.redhat.io credentials, ~20 GB free disk. Step 3 blocks in live mode; run it in a second terminal.
items.what_you_learn: Pull the signed Red Hat AI Inference Server (vLLM) image, download the validated RedHatAI/granite-3.3-8b-instruct model, serve it on localhost, and classify a real taxpayer refund inquiry without any inference call leaving the host.
highlights: ss -ltnp shows 127.0.0.1:8000 — the endpoint has no egress path; that screen is the point
podman pull prints 'Signature verified — policy: signedBy release key' on the way in
The curl reply returns category, routing queue, missing Form 8822 and a draft for a human to sign
assets/inquiry.json's system prompt forbids stating a determination as final

items.title: Lab 02 — Teach it your notice taxonomy
items.audience: Subject matter experts and data leads who own notice families, routing rules and correspondence house style
items.minutes: About 6 minutes (5 steps); hours of GPU to run live
items.prerequisites: LAB_MODE=simulate: only python3 (and only checked in live mode). LAB_MODE=live: a GPU host, Python with the sdg-hub and training-hub libraries, the Lab 01 endpoint (http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1) running as the teacher model, and several hours of GPU time. Note: check_seeds.py, generate.py, train.py and evaluate.py are not shipped in the lab directory — only taxonomy/knowledge/gov/tax/notices/qna.yaml is.
items.what_you_learn: Write agency knowledge as reviewable seed YAML (qna.yaml, schema v3), validate it, expand 12 seed examples into ~2,200 kept samples with SDG Hub, LoRA-tune Granite with Training Hub, and prove the tuned model beats the base.
highlights: 12 seed examples become 2,556 generated, 2,203 kept — every sample traces to a human-written seed
Evaluation table: notice family accuracy 0.61 → 0.94, cites the right form 0.44 → 0.89
check_seeds.py is the CI gate: fail in a pull request, not after four hours of GPU
Keep the held-out evaluation set out of the seed data or the numbers mean nothing

items.title: Lab 03 — Survive filing season
items.audience: Platform engineers and capacity planners responsible for taxpayer-facing services at April peak
items.prerequisites: LAB_MODE=simulate: nothing. LAB_MODE=live: an OpenShift cluster with Red Hat OpenShift AI installed, GPU nodes with the NVIDIA GPU Operator, oc authenticated, and hey for the load test. WARNING: step 6 consumes every GPU the namespace can schedule for 90 seconds — non-production cluster only.
items.what_you_learn: Deploy the Lab 02 model as a KServe InferenceService on the vllm-runtime, watch it become Ready in ~96 seconds, then run a 400-concurrent-user rehearsal and watch replicas climb 2 → 20 and back with no application change.
highlights: hey -z 90s -c 400: 1,183 req/s, p95 0.612s, zero errors, replicas 2 → 20 → 2
manifests/inferenceservice-tax-classifier.yaml is the capacity plan: minReplicas 2, scaleMetric concurrency, scaleTarget 24
storageUri pinned to sha256:4b91c0e2f7a3 — the digest the authorizing official approved, not a tag
Scale-to-two, not zero: cold-starting an 8B model costs ~90 seconds

items.title: Lab 04 — Ground answers in your own guidance
items.audience: Governance boards, correspondence reviewers and anyone deciding whether an AI answer may reach a taxpayer
items.prerequisites: LAB_MODE=simulate: nothing. LAB_MODE=live: an OpenShift cluster, psycopg installed, an embeddings endpoint (Lab 01 or Lab 03; default http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/embeddings), and your own guidance in labs/lab04-rag/corpus/ as .txt/.md/.adoc/.html. ingest.py --dry-run chunks a corpus with no database.
items.what_you_learn: Stand up pgvector on the same cluster as the model, ingest Publications 17/501/594 plus internal notice guidance (3,135 chunks), get a cited CP14 answer, then watch the system refuse a 2031 question and show exactly why.
highlights: The refusal: 'sources: none above threshold (0.75)' — refer to a specialist, exit code 3
--explain prints every rejected candidate with its score against the 0.750 threshold
Every good answer carries a sources block: Publication 594 p.4, score 0.891
The corpus is queried, never learned — sensitive text stays out of training
The run.sh has a fifth step, the --explain trace; the deck version stops at four

items.title: Lab 05 — Automate the toil around the model
items.audience: Operations and automation teams; whoever gets paged when inference saturates
items.prerequisites: LAB_MODE=simulate: nothing. LAB_MODE=live: Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform 2.4+, ansible-navigator and ansible-rulebook on the path (the rules engine needs a JDK), the ansible.eda collection, an Automation Controller with the named job templates, and Alertmanager posting to the rulebook source on port 5000.
items.what_you_learn: Run a health playbook that tests the endpoint the way a taxpayer would (including the served-digest check against CR-8841), then start an Event-Driven Ansible rulebook and watch a queue-depth alert remediated in 62 seconds with an audit row.
highlights: Alert 14:38:02 → job 40213 scales maxReplicas 20 → 32 → resolved 14:39:04. No ticket, no pager
rulebooks/inference_saturation.yml: ModelProvenanceMismatch deliberately escalates instead of self-remediating
awx job list shows launched_by eda-rulebook — the evidence Lab 06 asks for writes itself
The digest check is the task people forget; drift from the approved artefact is an accreditation finding

items.title: Lab 06 — Prove it to your ISSO
items.audience: ISSOs, authorizing officials, assessors and security architects accrediting an AI workload
items.prerequisites: LAB_MODE=simulate: nothing. LAB_MODE=live: oc authenticated to a cluster with the Compliance Operator and TrustyAI installed, cosign on the path, the agency model-signing public key (agency-model-signing.pub), and SSH access to a GPU node (default ocp-gpu-04). Step 2 reads node configuration over SSH.
items.what_you_learn: Run the four checks an authorizing official actually runs: cosign-verify the model against change record CR-8841, confirm FIPS and SELinux enforcing, read a real Compliance Operator result, and interpret TrustyAI drift and fairness metrics correctly.
highlights: oc get compliancescan: ocp4-moderate DONE NON-COMPLIANT — the honest result, and it is deliberate
1 of 217 checks failed (audit-log-forwarding); remediation available, or let the Lab 05 rulebook apply it
channel_mix drift 0.212 exceeds 0.150 — nothing is wrong with the model; more taxpayers moved to the portal
cosign verify names signer, timestamp and 'CR-8841 (approved by AO 2026-08-20)' before admission

items.title: Lab 07 — Ask your own logs
items.audience: SREs, on-call engineers and platform leads who own mean time to restore
items.prerequisites: LAB_MODE=simulate: nothing. LAB_MODE=live: an OpenShift cluster with OpenShift Logging (Loki), the Lab 04 vector store and model serving in place, logcli and python3 on the path. Note: ingest_ops.py and mttr_report.py are not shipped in the lab directory — only run.sh is.
items.what_you_learn: Point the Lab 04 retrieval pattern at operations: ingest 90 days of Loki logs, 48 runbooks, 312 postmortems and 1,240 change records (12,135 chunks), get a cited diagnosis of an OOM incident, remediate via Lab 05, and read the MTTR case.
highlights: Cited diagnosis in seconds: CR-9012 raised max_model_len 8192 → 16384; precedent INC-2209; runbook RB-114 steps 3-5
MTTR decomposition: diagnose 2h 41m → 24m; total 3h 16m → 59m (-70%)
Same stack as Lab 04 — only the corpus changed; nothing left the cluster
Logs carry hostnames and case identifiers: keeping this notebook on-cluster is not optional

items.title: Interactive deck — Labs view
items.audience: Self-guided readers and workshop attendees who want to type the commands themselves in a browser
items.minutes: Seven labs, roughly five minutes each
items.rung: Data · Information · Knowledge · Judgement (each lab card carries its own chip)
items.prerequisites: A browser. Open the deck with #labs on the URL, or #lab-3 to land on a specific lab; the sidebar Labs button does the same.
items.what_you_learn: All seven labs as virtual terminals: press Show to reveal the next command and type it, Run to execute it, or Demo to play one lab hands-free. Commands are real and copyable; output matches the run.sh scripts.
highlights: Seven terminal cards; the sidebar rail lists lab titles and scrolls to each card
Tab completes the next command like a shell; Show / Run / Demo buttons per lab
Deck's Lab 04 has 4 steps (no --explain trace) — the run.sh has 5
Closing card: nothing in seven labs required a public model endpoint or internet at inference time

items.title: Interactive deck — Demo view
items.audience: Kiosk screens, booth loops and anyone who wants to watch all seven labs play themselves
items.minutes: Loops through all seven labs continuously; speed 1×, 1.6×, 2.4× or 4×
items.rung: All four rungs (each lab's chip shown in the header as it plays)
items.prerequisites: A browser. Open the deck with #demo on the URL to start in Demo view already playing; otherwise press the sidebar Demo button.
items.what_you_learn: An automated walkthrough that types each lab's commands and prints the representative output, then shows the takeaway and moves to the next lab — the whole hands-on track without touching the keyboard.
highlights: Space plays/pauses; ← → switch labs; Restart lab and a Speed selector up to 4×
Header shows lab badge, product chip, time chip and rung chip; progress reads 'lab 3/7 · step 2 / 6'
Playback is clock-driven, so a throttled hidden tab drops smoothness but never pace
Ends each lab with '✓ Lab NN complete' and its Takeaway line, then loops

items.title: README — the kit in one page
items.what_you_learn: What the repository holds (seven labs, docs, deck, exports, bin/), the three-command quick start, the seven-lab table with product and rung, the two lab modes, and the honesty note about sample content.
highlights: Quick start: ./bin/preflight.sh, then LAB_PACE=step ./labs/lab01-rhel-ai/run.sh, then ./bin/run-all-labs.sh — no cluster, GPU or credentials.
Lab table: 01 AI Inference Server, 02 SDG Hub + Training Hub, 03 OpenShift AI, 04 pgvector, 05 Ansible, 06 Compliance/TrustyAI/Sigstore, 07 Logging.
Warning: LAB_MODE=live in Lab 03 consumes every GPU its namespace can schedule; Lab 06 reads node config over SSH.
Licence is MIT; the material is event enablement, not an official Red Hat product or publication.
items.audience: Anyone opening the repo cold — the first thing to read.
items.prerequisites: None.

items.title: Docs master document — About this guide, who it is for, five outcomes, how to run
items.what_you_learn: The book that stitches every module into one page: reader-to-lab routing, the five event outcomes mapped to labs, the env-variable table, and the Demo-view tip for hands-free playback.
highlights: Who this is for: 5 reader rows — platform (01,03,05), data/app (02,04), ops/SRE (07), security (06), programme leads (brief only).
Five outcomes table maps each abstract promise to the lab that proves it: 05, 01+02, 04, 06, 03.
Env table: LAB_MODE simulate, LAB_PACE auto, LAB_SPEED 0.04, NO_COLOR unset.
Includes 00-event-brief, labs 01–07 and 90-facilitator-guide at :leveloffset: +1, so each becomes a chapter.
items.audience: Self-guided readers choosing where to start.
items.prerequisites: None.

items.title: The ladder: data → information → knowledge → judgement
items.what_you_learn: The four-rung definitions that every slide, lab and product in the kit is tagged with, plus the 23-row table mapping each technology to the rung it serves.
highlights: Data = what happened; Information = data in context for one case; Knowledge = guidance, precedent, runbooks; Judgement = a determination someone signs.
Arrow form (data → information) marks a converter; 'executes judgement' marks automation carrying out a decision already made.
Table has 23 rows: RHEL data; AI Inference Server data → information; OpenShift AI information + knowledge; Model registry, Sigstore, Human reviewer judgement.
Ansible / Event-Driven Ansible = executes judgement; Compliance Operator and TrustyAI = information (evidence); llm-d and Models-as-a-Service = information.
items.audience: Everyone — it is the vocabulary the rest of the kit assumes.
items.prerequisites: None.

items.title: Event brief — operating reality, lifecycle map, architecture, AO questions, adoption path
items.what_you_learn: Why tax administration suits language models yet punishes normal deployment, where AI lands in the filing lifecycle, the four-layer reference architecture with two vertical concerns, and a 0–90–180-day adoption path.
highlights: Four realities: demand is seasonal, rules are locked in legacy code, answers are in the text, the data cannot leave (FTI).
Six-stage lifecycle table; only Exam selection is marked No — governance first, automation much later.
Seven questions an authorizing official asks, each mapped to a control and a lab (01, 04 or 06).
Prove days 0–90, Ground 90–180, Scale 180+; most programmes stall on the capacity plan and written data-class agreement.
items.audience: Programme and acquisition leads, ISSOs, anyone briefing leadership.
items.prerequisites: The ladder definitions.

items.title: Facilitator guide — running the 60-minute session
items.what_you_learn: Minute-by-minute timing for a 60-minute virtual event, which labs to run live and why, projector settings, the five planted questions, six stock answers, and a four-item honesty checklist.
highlights: Timing: slides 0–34 min, Lab 01 live 34–42 (stop on ss -ltnp), Lab 05 live 42–50 (the 62-second remediation), Q&A 56–60.
30-minute cut: slides 1, 2, 8, Lab 01, and the drift section of Lab 06; keep slide 17 loaded for ISSOs.
Projector: LAB_SPEED=0.08 LAB_PACE=step, or NO_COLOR=1 if screen share mangles ANSI; 80 columns is enough.
Say out loud: sample notices are illustrative, numbers are representative, exam selection is deliberately excluded, a human signs everything.
items.audience: Whoever presents or re-runs the session; attendees do not need it.
items.prerequisites: Have run ./bin/run-all-labs.sh once and opened slides/deck.html.
items.rung: judgement (keeps the human on the signature)

items.title: Shared AsciiDoc attributes — product names and lab defaults
items.what_you_learn: The single place product names and environment defaults are defined, so a rename is one edit; explains the {rhaiis}-style tokens seen throughout docs/.
highlights: Product tokens: rhel, rhaiis (Red Hat AI Inference Server), ocp, rhoai, aap, eda (Event-Driven Ansible).
Lab defaults: ns tax-inference, base-model granite-3.3-8b-instruct, tuned-model granite-8b-tax-v1, change-record CR-8841.
Rendering: :toc: left, :sectnums:, :sectanchors:, rouge highlighter, :idprefix: empty, :idseparator: - (so auto ids are plain kebab-case).
repo-url attribute points at https://github.com/nommsweyMX/redhat-ai-tax-labs.
items.audience: Contributors editing docs or adapting the kit to their own estate.
items.prerequisites: None.

items.title: Makefile — build docs, slides, PPTX, PDF and run the smoke test
items.what_you_learn: Ten targets that turn the AsciiDoc sources into the published site, using the docker.io/asciidoctor/docker-asciidoctor:latest container so Ruby is never installed locally.
highlights: docs → build/index.html; slides → build/slides.html (reveal.js 4.6.1 from jsdelivr); pdf → build/redhat-ai-tax-administration.pdf from docs/index.adoc.
pptx → python3 bin/build-pptx.py --out slides/exports/redhat-ai-tax-administration.pptx (needs only python-pptx).
lint = bash -n on bin/*.sh and labs/*/run.sh plus py_compile; test = lint then LAB_SPEED=0 NO_COLOR=1 ./bin/run-all-labs.sh.
RUNTIME picks podman or docker; check-runtime prints the local fallback asciidoctor -D build docs/index.adoc.
items.audience: Contributors and anyone rebuilding the site locally.
items.prerequisites: podman or docker for docs/slides/pdf; python3 + python-pptx for pptx; nothing for test.

items.title: bin/lib.sh — the shared lab runtime (simulate vs live)
items.what_you_learn: How every lab is a sequence of step calls — a real command plus its expected output — and how four environment variables switch mode, pacing, speed and colour.
highlights: Defaults from the file: LAB_MODE=simulate, LAB_PACE=auto, LAB_SPEED=0.04; NO_COLOR unset (any value, or a non-tty stdout, disables colour).
step "cmd" <<'OUT' ... OUT: simulate prints expected lines; live evals the command and on non-zero exit shows the expected output as the finding.
LAB_PACE=step prompts '[Enter] to run, s to skip, q to quit'; LAB_STEPS_TOTAL and LAB_PROMPT are per-lab knobs.
require_cmd exits 2 in live mode when a tool is missing; lab_footer returns 1 if any live step failed.
items.audience: Facilitators tuning a demo, and anyone writing a new lab.
items.prerequisites: bash.

items.title: bin/preflight.sh — which labs can run live here
items.what_you_learn: A never-failing readiness report: for each of the seven labs it lists the CLI tools LAB_MODE=live needs and prints 'live ready' or 'simulate only (missing: ...)'.
highlights: lab01 needs podman huggingface-cli curl jq; lab03 needs oc curl jq hey; lab05 needs ansible-navigator ansible-rulebook.
lab06 needs oc cosign ssh; lab07 needs logcli python3; lab02 and lab04 need python3 (lab04 also oc).
Ends by reminding that every lab runs today in simulate mode via ./bin/run-all-labs.sh.
It is the first command in the README quick start.
items.audience: Anyone about to run a lab, especially before a live session.
items.prerequisites: bash.

items.title: bin/run-all-labs.sh — walk all seven labs end to end
items.what_you_learn: The rehearsal and CI smoke test: cds into each labs/lab*/ directory, runs run.sh, counts failures and exits 1 if any lab failed.
highlights: Exports LAB_MODE (default simulate) so it can also drive a full live run.
Step totals per lab from run.sh: 01=5, 02=5, 03=6, 04=5, 05=4, 06=5, 07=5 (35 steps).
CI and make test call it with LAB_SPEED=0 NO_COLOR=1 for a fast, plain-text run.
Prints '>>> labNN' before each lab and 'All labs completed.' at the end.
items.audience: Facilitators rehearsing; contributors before a pull request.
items.prerequisites: bash; nothing else in simulate mode.

items.title: bin/build-pptx.py — generate the PowerPoint export with native shapes
items.what_you_learn: A 652-line python-pptx script that builds a 10-slide 16:9 deck with speaker notes and editable graphics rather than screenshots, using the same palette as the HTML deck.
highlights: Native drawings: a cosine-interpolated filing-season demand curve, a six-chevron lifecycle flow, a layered architecture, a three-phase roadmap.
Palette matches deck.html: Red Hat red #CC0000 plus the rainbow rung scale (red, orange, green, violet); fonts Red Hat Display/Text/Mono.
Slide 2 draws the ladder as a rising staircase of four rung cards with technology captions.
Usage: python3 bin/build-pptx.py [--out slides/exports/redhat-ai-tax-administration.pptx]; requires pip install python-pptx.
items.audience: Contributors regenerating the export after changing the narrative.
items.prerequisites: python3 and python-pptx (1.0.2 is installed here).

items.title: PowerPoint export — redhat-ai-tax-administration.pptx
items.what_you_learn: The upload-friendly deck for platforms and review processes that insist on .pptx: 10 slides with speaker notes covering the ladder, operating reality, lifecycle, outcomes, architecture, adoption, next steps, labs and AO questions.
highlights: Verified with python-pptx: 10 slides, 67,282 bytes; the reveal/HTML decks carry 17 slides, so this is a condensed cut.
Slide titles include 'From data to judgement — and who climbs each step' and 'The questions an authorizing official will ask'.
Speaker notes carry the same talk beats: stop Lab 01 on step 4 (127.0.0.1), the demand-curve argument, exam selection is gray.
Regenerate with make pptx; CI copies slides/exports/ to /exports/ on the site.
items.audience: Event platforms, agency reviewers, anyone who needs a file not a URL.
items.prerequisites: PowerPoint or LibreOffice.

items.title: Printable PDF — the whole documentation book
items.what_you_learn: The same content as /docs/index.html — brief, seven lab modules, facilitator guide — rendered by asciidoctor-pdf for offline or air-gapped reading.
highlights: Built by make pdf and by the CI build job: asciidoctor-pdf -D build -o redhat-ai-tax-administration.pdf docs/index.adoc.
Source is the documentation, not the slides; the slide deck's PDF-equivalent is the .pptx export.
Not committed to the repo; it exists only in build/ and on the published site.
items.audience: Readers in disconnected enclaves or who print.
items.prerequisites: None.

items.title: slides/slides.adoc — the reveal.js deck with speaker notes
items.what_you_learn: The 17-slide event narrative as asciidoctor-revealjs source: AI in plain English, why now, inside an LLM, the ladder, where AI lands, five outcomes, architecture, why Red Hat AI, one platform, ops loop, logs-to-MTTR, adoption, next steps, labs, security appendix.
highlights: Every slide opens with a monospace 'Rung: ...' line and closes with a [.notes] block — 17 of each; press S in the browser for notes.
Header: Red Hat · Four Inc. · Carahsoft virtual event, September 17, 2026, presented by Jon Keam and Brad Scalio.
Slide 13 'Point the same pattern at your logs — MTTR is the proof' is the ops-notebook argument that Lab 07 demonstrates.
Built with asciidoctor-revealjs at 1280×720, white theme, fade transition, slide numbers c/t.
items.audience: Presenters and readers who want the narrative in order.
items.prerequisites: A browser.

items.title: slides/ladder-map.json — the rung tagging source of truth
items.what_you_learn: The machine-readable theme: four rungs with colours and CSS classes, per-slide rung lists and item tags for all 17 slides, the seven lab chips, and 23 technology mappings the docs table mirrors.
highlights: Rungs in rainbow order: data #CC0000 r-data, information #C2410C r-info, knowledge #1E7A55 r-know, judgement #5B2E91 r-judge — yellow and blue are only the in-between segments of the ladder track.
Chip conventions: plain ('Knowledge'), arrow ('data → information'), automation ('executes judgement'); CSS for the pill is included.
Slide 14 note records the mapping prove/ground/scale = data/information/knowledge, verbatim from the Sept 3 planning call.
deck.html, presenter-notes.html, slides.adoc, docs/ and README must agree with it; bin/build-adventure.py reads it to build this page.
items.audience: Contributors changing the theme or adding a slide, lab or product.
items.prerequisites: None.

items.title: .github/workflows/docs.yml — test, build and publish to GitHub Pages
items.what_you_learn: Three chained jobs: lint and run every lab in simulate mode, build docs/slides/PDF in the asciidoctor container, then deploy build/ to Pages — only on a push to main.
highlights: test: bash -n over bin/*.sh and labs/*/run.sh, py_compile, then ./bin/run-all-labs.sh with LAB_SPEED=0 NO_COLOR=1 — labs gate the docs.
build: docs/index.html, slides.html, redhat-ai-tax-administration.pdf, then stages deck.html as index.html (and /deck.html), presenter-notes.html, adventure.html and slides/exports/ into build/.
publish: actions/configure-pages@v5, upload-pages-artifact@v3, deploy-pages@v4; concurrency group docs-${{ github.ref }}.
Only a push to main publishes; pull requests run the test and build jobs without deploying.
items.audience: Maintainers; anyone wondering why a push did or did not publish.
items.prerequisites: Repo write access to trigger.

items.title: labs/lab04-rag/ingest.py — chunk, embed and index guidance into pgvector
items.what_you_learn: A deliberately boring ingestion pipeline: fixed-window chunks with overlap that prefer paragraph breaks, embedded via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and upserted into a pgvector table with an HNSW cosine index.
highlights: Defaults: --source ./corpus, --chunk 800, --overlap 120, --embed-model granite-embedding-125m, --batch 32; reads .txt .md .adoc .html .htm.
--dry-run (used in the lab) walks the corpus and reports chunk counts with no psycopg, endpoint or database.
Creates table tax_guidance(uid, source, ordinal, body, embedding vector(768)) and index tax_guidance_hnsw with vector_cosine_ops.
Env: EMBED_ENDPOINT default http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/embeddings; PGHOST PGPORT PGDATABASE(tax_guidance) PGUSER PGPASSWORD.
items.audience: Data and application teams building retrieval over published guidance.
items.prerequisites: python3; for live, psycopg[binary], pgvector (manifests/pgvector.yaml) and the Lab 01 or 03 endpoint.

items.title: labs/lab04-rag/query.py — cited answers, and the refusal that is the point
items.what_you_learn: Retrieval-augmented answering where the important behaviour is refusing: below a relevance threshold it says it has no guidance, recommends referral, and exits 3 so a workflow can route to a human.
highlights: RELEVANCE_THRESHOLD = 0.75, TOP_K = 6; score is 1 - cosine distance from pgvector's <=> operator.
--explain prints the retrieval trace — every candidate, its score, accepted/REJECTED, the threshold and the decision — for a governance board.
System prompt has four rules: only the passages, cite every claim, say so and refer if unanswered, never state a taxpayer determination as final.
Defaults: --model granite-8b-tax-v1, temperature 0.1, max_tokens 600, INFERENCE_ENDPOINT http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions.
items.audience: Data teams and governance staff asking how hallucination is stopped.
items.prerequisites: Indexed corpus from ingest.py; psycopg; a chat-completions endpoint (live only).

items.title: labs/lab04-rag/corpus/ — the empty guidance drop zone
items.what_you_learn: Where your own published guidance goes before a live ingest, and why the repo ships it empty: agency material must never be committed to a public repository.
highlights: README.txt is a one-line placeholder: drop published guidance here (PDF, HTML or text).
gitignore excludes labs/lab04-rag/corpus/* except README.txt; sdg/, checkpoints/ and .venv/ under labs are also ignored.
ingest.py only reads .txt .md .adoc .html .htm — PDFs must be converted first.
items.audience: Anyone preparing a live run of Lab 04.
items.prerequisites: Your agency's published guidance.

items.title: Notice taxonomy seed — qna.yaml for SDG Hub
items.what_you_learn: What a subject-matter expert actually writes to teach a model agency vocabulary: short contexts plus question/answer pairs in the qna.yaml taxonomy format, reviewed like code.
highlights: version 3, domain tax_administration, created_by revenue-modernization-team; 4 seed contexts and 9 question/answer pairs (docs say '12 seed examples').
Contexts: CP2000 is a proposal not a bill (30 days, Automated Underreporter); CP14 first balance notice with four payment options.
Third context: refund inquiry after a move — Form 8822 first, then the refund trace; fourth: house style, one action per paragraph.
Memorable line: 'The model drafts; it never sends' — a named reviewer edits and signs every reply.
items.audience: Data teams and the SMEs who will write the real taxonomy.
items.prerequisites: None to read; SDG Hub and Training Hub plus GPU hours to use.

items.title: .gitattributes and .gitignore — LF enforcement and what never gets committed
items.what_you_learn: Why the lab scripts run identically on every machine: every textual file is forced to LF, and lab working directories and the guidance corpus are excluded from git.
highlights: * text=auto eol=lf, with explicit LF for .sh .py .yml .yaml .adoc .json .ini and Makefile; .pptx .png .pdf binary.
Ignored: build/, __pycache__, labs/*/sdg/, labs/*/checkpoints/, labs/*/.venv/, labs/lab04-rag/corpus/* (except README.txt).
Rationale in the file: CRLF in a shell script is a runtime error that only shows up on someone else's machine.
items.audience: Contributors.
items.prerequisites: None.

items.title: AI foundations for intelligent tax administration
items.audience: Anyone starting the kit
items.what_you_learn: The framing of the hour and the four-rung ladder legend (data, information, knowledge, judgement) that every later slide and lab is tagged with.
highlights: The promise: every claim made today gets run in a shell before you leave.
Legend: judgement is 'a determination someone signs' — deliberately human; automation executes it.
Presented by Jon Keam and Brad Scalio; hosts Red Hat, Four Inc., Carahsoft; September 17, 2026.

items.title: Four different jobs get called “AI”
items.what_you_learn: Predictive, generative/LLM, agentic and automation defined as four separate jobs, each with a plain analogy, its ladder rung, and a 'what it is not' box.
highlights: Analogies: weather forecast, well-read drafting assistant, junior analyst with a restricted tool belt, checklist that performs itself.
Not-box: an LLM is not a database, policy authority or source of truth; an agent is not permission to bypass controls.
Notes: automation is the prerequisite — 'if you are not automated' you will not have good AI inside your boundary.

items.title: The work is seasonal, textual and unforgiving
items.what_you_learn: Why tax agencies are the case: April demand at 6× the August low against fixed staff, rules locked in legacy code, unstructured text, and FTI rules that forbid public endpoints.
highlights: Chart title: a year of demand arrives in six weeks — the shaded gap is what automation absorbs.
The constraint that decides everything: the data cannot leave — the model comes to the data.
Console pivot line: choosing a model is a six-month decision; where it runs is a ten-year one.

items.title: An LLM is the engine — not the whole vehicle
items.what_you_learn: The six-layer stack around a model (mission app → context/RAG → model → inference → platform → compute + data) and the three knobs: prompting, RAG, fine-tuning.
highlights: Fine-tuning is studying for the test. Retrieval is bringing the notebook. You want both.
The model is learned language patterns — not your live system of record.
Inference is vLLM, the Red Hat AI Inference Server; platform is RHEL and OpenShift AI.

items.title: From data to judgement — and who climbs each step
items.what_you_learn: The ladder as a staircase: predictive AI climbs data→information, generative AI with RAG climbs to knowledge, and only people climb to judgement.
highlights: The top step is marked 'stays human' — a design rule, not a technical limit.
The backlog lives at the bottom of the ladder; every hour absorbed there is an examiner hour.
Console calls this the masterpiece slide: if the room remembers one picture, make it this one.

items.title: Predictive and generative AI answer different questions
items.minutes: 3–11 block (optional; first to cut if running long)
items.what_you_learn: A five-row table (learns from / produces / in tax terms / fails as / governed by) plus a Venn showing how the two compose on one platform.
highlights: Predictive fails as a bad number; generative fails as a plausible sentence — so grounding and review are non-negotiable.
Governed by: back-testing and fairness metrics vs retrieval with citations, sign-off and drift — Labs 04 · 06.
The score picks the case, the language model prepares the brief, a person decides.

items.title: Where AI actually lands in the filing lifecycle
items.what_you_learn: Six lifecycle stages; intake, validation, correspondence, collections support and taxpayer service are AI-assisted with a human in the loop, while exam selection is held back.
highlights: Exam selection is deliberately NOT highlighted — 'governance first'; saying so unprompted buys credibility.
Rule of thumb: start where a human already reviews the output.
Rule of thumb: automate the toil around the model, not just the model.

items.title: Five outcomes, and where each one is proven
items.what_you_learn: The five event-abstract outcomes, each mapped to the Red Hat product that delivers it and the lab that proves it — the map of the rest of the hour.
highlights: Modernize operations → Ansible Automation Platform · Event-Driven Ansible · OpenShift → Labs 05 · 07.
Efficiency → AI Inference Server, SDG Hub + Training Hub → Labs 01–02; insights → OpenShift AI, vector store, Llama Stack → Lab 04.
Security → RHEL · Compliance Operator · TrustyAI · Sigstore → Lab 06; foundation → OpenShift AI · KServe · vLLM → Lab 03.

items.title: One foundation, from bare metal to the taxpayer
items.what_you_learn: The reference architecture: RHEL + AI Inference Server on GPU nodes, OpenShift, OpenShift AI (serving, training, pipelines, registry, retrieval), mission apps — with trust and automation pillars spanning every layer.
highlights: Most failures happen at the seams between systems, not inside them — the platform makes seams boring.
Trust pillar (Lab 06) and automation pillar (Lab 05) are not a layer you add at the end.
Systems of record stay where they are — reached through APIs and automation, not replaced.

items.title: The federal problem is not “get a model.” It is operate AI without giving up control.
items.what_you_learn: The Red Hat proposition and six take-home proof points: model freedom, data locality, Models-as-a-Service, accelerator efficiency, predictive + generative lifecycle, Ansible closes the loop.
highlights: Bring the model to the mission — not the mission data to somebody else's model.
A glass box you can open and inspect, not a black box.
Models-as-a-Service: a central platform team publishes governed endpoints other projects consume.

items.title: Define the service once — run it wherever the mission needs it
items.what_you_learn: One InferenceService manifest with a signed model, delivered by GitOps, deploys unchanged (oc apply) to a datacenter, an accredited cloud region, or an air-gapped enclave.
highlights: Placement is policy, not re-architecture — moving a workload is a redeploy of the same manifest.
Accredit once, inherit everywhere; April becomes a scheduling event on pooled GPUs (Lab 03).
Notes: modern lock-in limits FUTURE decisions — the phone plan that can only call Domino's.

items.title: The useful pattern is a loop, not a chatbot
items.what_you_learn: The operations flywheel — predict, explain, ground + act, learn — with predictive ML, the LLM, RAG and Ansible each doing the one job it is good at.
highlights: Do not let fluency become authority — telemetry and retrieved sources decide whether the explanation holds.
Generated content is a draft until it passes the same curation as any other knowledge record.
Example: GPU queue depth abnormal → LLM explains → RAG cites the runbook → Event-Driven Ansible scales after approval.

items.title: Point the same pattern at your logs — MTTR is the proof
items.what_you_learn: The Lab 04 retrieval stack aimed at logs, runbooks, incidents and change records; mean time to resolution decomposed before and after an on-cluster ops notebook.
highlights: Before 3h 16m (diagnose 2h 41m); with the notebook 59m (diagnose 24m) — diagnosis -84%.
Detect, fix and verify are unchanged — the hours lived in diagnosis.
Logs are FTI-adjacent, so the notebook runs on the same OpenShift it observes; Lab 07 runs it end to end.

items.title: Ninety days, then ninety more
items.what_you_learn: A crawl/walk/run adoption path — Prove (days 0–90), Ground (90–180), Scale (180+) — with five concrete checklist items per phase.
highlights: Prove = data, Ground = information, Scale = knowledge.
Agencies stall on Crawl's second and third bullets: no accelerator capacity plan, no written data-class agreement.
Measure the baseline before you change anything; report outcomes in mission terms, not token counts.

items.title: What happens after this hour
items.what_you_learn: Three concrete asks — a half-day architecture workshop, a guided pilot with a measured baseline, and acquisition through Four Inc. and Carahsoft — plus the repo and contact strip.
highlights: If you did not see it here, that does not mean it does not exist — ask.
Foundational questions are free to ask and expensive to skip.
Whole kit lives at github.com/nommsweyMX/redhat-ai-tax-labs.

items.title: Seven labs — real commands, run them yourself
items.what_you_learn: The seven lab cards with their rung chips and one-line goals — the deck's concluding takeaway before the presenter switches to the Labs view.
highlights: Run this on a personal laptop — never production, never a work laptop.
One thing to remember: nothing needed a public endpoint, internet at inference time, or a system-of-record rewrite.
Console plan: run Lab 01 live (stop hard on ss -ltnp) and Lab 05 live (the 62-second remediation).

items.title: The questions an authorizing official will ask
items.audience: ISSOs, security leads, authorizing officials
items.what_you_learn: The security appendix: eight questions an authorizing official actually asks, each mapped to a platform control and where it lives.
highlights: Parked in the appendix on purpose — but this is the slide that unblocks the deal.
Evidence is information; the authorizing official's decision is judgement.
Pull it up together with Lab 06 the moment an ISSO engages.

items.title: Presenter console
anchors: 24 <section class="step"> steps: Slide 01–17 / 17, then Lab 01–07 · hands-on
localStorage key ptc-pos remembers your step
items.rung: all four (each step carries its rung chips and an 'On the ladder' beat)
items.audience: Presenters; self-guided readers who want the full talk track
items.what_you_learn: The talk track behind every slide and lab: what is on screen, what to say, the five planted questions, per-command 'say' lines for all seven labs, and the ladder mapping per step.
highlights: Run of show: slides 0–34 min, Lab 01 live 34–42, Lab 05 live 42–50, skim the rest 50–56, questions 56–60.
Only 30 minutes? Slides 1, 2, 8 plus Lab 01 and the drift section of Lab 06.
Delivery rule: goal number one is to entertain — a tuned-out audience learns nothing.
Keys: ← → or Space to move, J jump, M read-all; Home/End; 'Read all' shows every step on one page.

items.title: PLANTED: “So is AI taking our jobs?”
anchors: lands on slide-05 'From data to judgement'
items.what_you_learn: Jon asks; Brad answers that AI is not coming for your job because right now it does not have judgement — the ladder's top step stays human.
highlights: The make-the-tests-pass story: told to make tests pass, the AI edits the code until they do — information, not judgement.
Optional garnish, attributed to Karpathy: you can outsource intelligence but not understanding.

items.title: PLANTED: “What’s a seam?”
anchors: lands on slide-09 'One foundation, from bare metal to the taxpayer'
items.what_you_learn: Jon plays the foil; Brad answers with the pants analogy — failures happen at integration seams between systems, never in the middle where the fabric is strongest.
highlights: RHEL and OpenShift interoperating layer to layer is what makes the seams boring.
'We are not the only ones who do it — but we are uniquely positioned.'

items.title: PLANTED: “What is fine-tuning to you, Jon?”
anchors: lands on slide-09; answer draws on slide-04's test/notebook line
items.what_you_learn: Brad cold-asks Jon on the architecture slide; the answer reprises 'fine-tuning is studying for the test, retrieval is bringing the notebook' and turns information into actionable knowledge.
highlights: Jon calls 'how do you turn information into actionable knowledge' the core of the whole talk.
Fine-tuning is durable behavior — never facts that change each filing season.

items.title: PLANTED: “What do you actually mean by lock-in?”
anchors: lands on slide-11 'Define the service once'
items.what_you_learn: Jon plays the foil ('I thought we already bought the software'); Brad answers with the phone-plan analogy: modern lock-in limits future decisions without you knowing.
highlights: A plan where you cannot call Pizza Hut, only Domino's — real lock-in is bespoke hyperscaler-unique services.
Honest caveat said out loud: sometimes you legitimately need a native service; the ask is only infrastructure as code.

items.title: PLANTED: “What is a predicament versus a problem?”
anchors: lands on slide-14 'Ninety days, then ninety more'
items.what_you_learn: Jon asks; Brad answers that a problem you solve today while a predicament you can only plan around — so a hypothetical GPU shortage must not stall the pilot.
highlights: Plan for problems, not predicaments: the problem now is grounding the proof so you can scale.
Success test: no decision made today may limit your options tomorrow.

items.title: AO questions table (security appendix)
anchors: slide-17 <table class="grid"> — columns: Their question · The platform control · Where it lives
items.audience: ISSOs, authorizing officials, security leads
items.what_you_learn: Eight AO questions with the control that answers each: data locality, signed models, FIPS, FISMA moderate/high, continuous compliance, drift, disconnected operation, and human accountability.
highlights: Where does data go? Nowhere — AI Inference Server · OpenShift AI. Approved model? Signed and verified — Sigstore / cosign.
Crypto validated? RHEL FIPS mode. FISMA moderate/high? Controls map to NIST 800-53 baselines; FIPS 199 picks the venue.
Stays compliant? Compliance Operator scans. Drifting? TrustyAI metrics on live traffic.
No internet? oc-mirror · registry. Who is accountable? A named reviewer — the model drafts, it never sends.

items.title: Deck keyboard shortcuts and views
anchors: deckbar hint: '← → to move · N presenter notes · F present full-screen'
demo foot: 'Space plays and pauses · ← → switch labs · loops through all seven continuously. Open the page with #demo on the URL to start here, playing.'
rail buttons: Deck / Labs / Demo; Notes toggle (deck view only); Present button
items.what_you_learn: How to drive the deck: three views (Deck, Labs, Demo), slide keys, the Notes panel that shows each slide's data-notes, and the virtual-terminal controls in the Labs view.
highlights: Deck view: ← → (also PageUp/PageDown) move, Home/End jump, N toggles presenter notes, F toggles full-screen stage.
Demo view: Space plays/pauses, ← → switch labs, speed 1× / 1.6× / 2.4× / 4×, loops all seven.
Labs view terminals: Show reveals the next command, Run executes it, Demo plays the lab; Enter submits, Tab completes, Copy all / Reset.
Off-script commands are refused — the terminal only accepts the lab's real, copyable commands.
items.prerequisites: Deep links: #slide-9 (or #9) opens a slide, #labs the Labs view, #lab-3 a specific lab, #demo the Demo view playing.
